summaries.example: Imagine your friend tells you that the library is open. You know your friend usually tells the truth, so you believe them. Now imagine a stranger says the same thing. Should you believe the stranger just as quickly? Philosophers use cases like these to ask what makes learning from another person reasonable.
summaries.summary: Testimony is one of the main ways people learn. When someone tells us that something is true, we often form a belief based on their words. The philosophical problem is to explain when that belief is reasonable or counts as knowledge. One debate is between reductionism and non-reductionism. Reductionists say the listener must have positive reasons for thinking the speaker is reliable. Global reductionists focus on whether testimony in general is reliable, while local reductionists focus on the particular speaker and situation. Non-reductionists say people have a defeasible, or easily defeated, permission to believe testimony unless they have a reason to doubt it. Hybrid views combine parts of both approaches, sometimes treating children differently from adults or giving both speaker and listener a role. Other debates ask whether knowledge is transmitted from a knowledgeable speaker or can be generated in the listener, what kind of evidence supports testimony, and whether the speaker’s assurance or reliable communication process matters instead. The entry also examines experts, groups, and the nature of testimony itself.
key_ideas: Much of what we know comes from other people, including facts about science, history, and the world around us.
Reductionists say listeners need positive, non-testimonial reasons for trusting a speaker. Non-reductionists say trust is usually allowed unless there is a reason to doubt.
Some philosophers think testimony passes knowledge from a speaker to a listener. Others think a listener can gain knowledge even when the speaker does not know the fact.
Philosophers also ask whether evidence comes from the listener, the speaker, the relationship between them, or reliable ways of producing and receiving information.
The same questions can apply to experts, groups, and reports made by organizations.
summaries.why_it_matters: No one can check every fact personally. We depend on parents, teachers, scientists, witnesses, friends, and many other speakers. Understanding testimony helps us avoid being too gullible while also recognizing that learning from others is necessary. It also helps us think carefully about experts, group reports, and information found online.

important_terms.definition: Learning or gaining information from what another person says, writes, or communicates.
A good reason for believing something. A belief is justified when it is reasonable to hold.
A reason that should make you stop trusting a claim, such as discovering that the speaker often makes things up.
The view that we need our own good reasons for thinking a speaker is reliable before testimony can justify us.
The view that we may normally accept what people tell us unless we have a good reason to doubt it.
A person whose knowledge or skill makes their report especially important in a certain subject.

questions_to_think_about: When should you trust a friend, teacher, stranger, or online writer?
Can a young child learn something reasonably from a parent without checking it first?
Does an expert’s report replace your other reasons, or should you add it to them?
Can a group know or testify to something even when no single member knows the whole claim?

summaries.example: Suppose a student asks a stranger for directions to a hotel. The stranger says it is three blocks away. A local reductionist may ask whether the student has non-testimonial reasons to regard this speaker as reliable on this occasion. A non-reductionist may say the student is initially entitled to accept the answer unless there is a defeater, such as a sign showing the stranger is disoriented. A hybrid theorist might hold that ordinary context supplies some support while the speaker’s actual reliability also matters.
summaries.summary: The entry examines how testimony—communication offered or received as information—can support justified belief and knowledge. Its first major dispute is reductionism versus non-reductionism. Reductionists endorse a positive-reasons requirement: a hearer must have non-testimonial grounds for treating the speaker as reliable and must lack undefeated reasons for doubt. Global reductionism concerns the reliability of testimony generally; local reductionism concerns the speaker and circumstances at hand. Global versions face circularity, regress, and impractical demands for independent confirmation. Local versions avoid some of these objections but appear to make it difficult for children or uninformed hearers to learn from ordinary testimony. Non-reductionists instead defend a presumptive entitlement to accept testimony in the absence of defeaters, though critics worry about gullibility. Hybrid theories assign different roles to speaker and hearer or combine weaker positive reasons with speaker reliability. The entry then considers whether testimony transmits knowledge from a knowledgeable speaker or can generate knowledge in a hearer, and whether testimonial justification depends on evidence, inherited justification, interpersonal assurance, reliable processes, or a combination. Further debates concern individualism and anti-individualism, authoritative testimony, group testimony, and competing accounts of what testimony itself is.
key_ideas: The central dispute asks whether testimonial justification is reducible to the hearer’s perception, memory, and inference, or whether testimony is a basic source of justification.

Global reductionism faces worries about circular reasoning, an endless regress, the burden of checking many facts, and treating all subject matters as equally reliable. Local reductionism avoids some of these problems but may make ordinary testimony, including children’s learning, too difficult to justify.

Non-reductionism explains everyday trust more easily but faces the worry that it permits irrational gullibility in cases involving anonymous or bizarre reports. Hybrid views try to balance trust and critical assessment.

The transmission view says the speaker must know what is communicated for the hearer to gain testimonial knowledge. Generation views allow that a hearer may know or be justified even when the speaker lacks knowledge or justification.

Accounts of testimonial justification appeal variously to the hearer’s evidence, evidence inherited from the speaker, interpersonal assurance, reliable production and reception, or combinations of these.

Individualist accounts explain testimony using only hearer-related features. Anti-individualist accounts hold that the speaker, other speakers, or the social environment can also be epistemically relevant.
summaries.why_it_matters: Testimony makes shared knowledge possible: people rely on communication for science, history, education, public information, and ordinary decisions. Yet dependence creates a tension. If we demand independent evidence for every report, learning from others becomes nearly impossible; if we accept reports without safeguards, we risk gullibility. The competing theories clarify what roles should be played by speaker competence, hearer judgment, context, evidence, trust, expertise, and social groups.

important_terms.definition: The epistemological study of how testimony can provide justification or knowledge.
The position that testimonial justification must be explained through other resources of the hearer, such as perception, memory, and inference.
Reductionism requiring reasons that testimony as a general practice is reliable.
Reductionism requiring reasons that a particular speaker is reliable in the relevant context or subject.
The position that testimony is a basic source of justification: a hearer may accept it unless an undefeated defeater gives reason for doubt.
A reason indicating that a claim is false or unlikely, and that has not itself been overcome by better information.
The claim that testimonial knowledge can only pass from a speaker who already knows the proposition.
The claim that the relevant reliability of testimony can produce justification through the processes by which testimony is produced and received.

questions_to_think_about: Does a person need evidence that testimony in general is reliable, or can the situation itself justify trust?
How should a theory explain a child’s ability to learn from a parent’s testimony?
If a speaker is accidentally correct but lacks knowledge, can the listener still know what was said?
Should an expert’s testimony replace a listener’s other reasons, or merely add a strong reason?
Can a group testify or know something that no individual member knows?

summaries.example: Your science teacher says that a certain plant should not be touched. You have learned that the teacher is careful about science, and the warning fits the situation, so you believe it. Later, an anonymous post says the same plant is harmless. Even if you cannot prove the post false, you may have reasons to be cautious. Philosophers disagree about whether your first belief needs positive evidence about the teacher or is reasonable simply because you have no good reason to doubt her.
summaries.summary: The entry studies the philosophical puzzles raised by testimony, which is our dependence on what others communicate. The main issue in the opening debate is whether testimonial justification is basic or reducible to other sources of justification. Reductionists say a hearer must possess positive, non-testimonial reasons for judging a speaker reliable and must not face an undefeated defeater. Global reductionists seek reasons that testimony in general tends to be reliable; local reductionists seek reasons concerning a particular speaker, subject, or occasion. Global theories risk circularity or regress because testimony may be needed to establish testimony’s reliability, and they may require far more independent checking than people can perform. Local theories avoid some of this but appear to make it hard for children and strangers to learn from testimony. Non-reductionists defend a presumptive right to accept what is said unless there is a reason to doubt it, while opponents say this can license gullibility. Hybrid theories combine limited trust with evidence about speakers or contexts. The entry also introduces the transmission and generation debate: whether testimonial knowledge must come from a speaker who knows, or whether testimony can sometimes generate knowledge for the hearer. Later issues include evidence, assurance, reliability, expertise, groups, and the definition of testimony.
key_ideas: Testimony is indispensable because people cannot personally investigate everything they need to know.
Reductionism demands positive reasons for trust. Global reductionism concerns testimony generally; local reductionism concerns a particular speaker and setting.

Critics of reductionism argue that independent checking may lead to circular reasoning, an endless chain of supporting reports, or unrealistic demands. Critics of non-reductionism worry that merely lacking doubt could make strange reports seem acceptable.
Hybrid theories attempt to preserve reasonable trust without permitting careless belief, including by considering the speaker’s reliability and the listener’s situation together.

A separate debate concerns whether the speaker’s knowledge must be passed on, or whether the listener can gain knowledge through testimony in cases where the speaker is mistaken, unjustified, or does not know.
Further theories ask whether testimony is evidence, an assurance between people, or the result of reliable processes. They also ask whether the speaker matters as much as the listener.
summaries.why_it_matters: Our knowledge is socially distributed. We learn from teachers, family, experts, institutions, witnesses, and one another. A good theory must explain both why accepting testimony is often rational and why some reports should be rejected. These questions are especially important when information is difficult to verify personally, when speakers disagree, or when a source claims special authority.

important_terms.definition: Information accepted from another person’s words, writing, or communication.
A belief supported well enough that holding it is reasonable.
A reason for thinking a claim is false or probably false; an undefeated defeater still has force against the belief.
The theory that a listener needs independent reasons to think a speaker is trustworthy before testimony justifies belief.
The theory that testimony normally gives a listener an initial right to believe, unless a reason to doubt defeats it.
A view combining parts of reductionism and non-reductionism, often giving speaker and listener separate roles.
The view that a listener can gain knowledge from testimony only when the speaker already knows the claim.
The view that testimony can produce knowledge or justification in the listener, even under some conditions where the speaker lacks it.

questions_to_think_about: Is not having a reason to doubt someone enough, or must you also have a reason to trust them?
Why might global reductionism be harder to defend than local reductionism?
Can a student know something from a teacher who happens to state a truth without knowing it?
How should we balance respect for an expert with our own evidence and reasoning?
When a group publishes a report, is the group itself a source of testimony?
